commands.name: strace
commands.summary: Trace system calls and signals made by a process.
commands.risk_reason: Can slow traced process significantly; read-only observation.
cautions: Attaching to a live process can slow it 2–50× and cause timeouts in production — time-box it and use -c for summaries.
Output may contain secrets (read/write buffers, environment).
commands.explanation: strace intercepts and logs every system call (open, read, write, socket, etc.) made by a process. The go-to tool for debugging 'permission denied' errors, missing files, and mysterious failures — shows exactly what the kernel sees.

flags.desc: Attach to an already-running process by PID
Write output to file instead of stderr

examples.desc: Trace network calls of running nginx
Find missing files a command tries to open
Get syscall frequency summary for PID 1234
Run app and log all syscalls to file

commands.pro_tip: Use `strace -e trace=openat,read,write` to narrow output — full strace output is overwhelming; filtering to file I/O syscalls finds 80% of 'permission denied' bugs fast.

commands.name: iotop
commands.summary: Interactive real-time display of disk I/O per process.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only monitor; requires root or CAP_NET_ADMIN.
cautions: Needs root and adds some overhead; -a/-o views are enough for most checks.
commands.explanation: iotop shows disk read/write rates per process in real time, similar to top for disk I/O. Invaluable for identifying which process is generating excessive disk activity that affects performance.

examples.desc: Show only processes actively doing I/O
Three batch snapshots of active I/O

commands.pro_tip: Run `iotop -o` when a system is slow and top shows high I/O wait — iotop immediately reveals which process is the I/O culprit without guessing.

commands.name: perf
commands.summary: Linux performance analysis and profiling tool.
commands.risk_reason: Profiling adds overhead; kernel tracing requires root.
cautions: Sampling at high frequency adds overhead on production hosts; keep runs short.
Recorded data can include process names, arguments and memory addresses — treat perf.data as sensitive.
commands.explanation: perf is the Linux performance profiling tool, using hardware counters and kernel tracepoints. It records CPU samples, tracks cache misses, counts system calls, and generates flame graphs. Essential for diagnosing performance bottlenecks at the CPU/kernel level.

flags.desc: Run command and print performance statistics
Format perf.data for flame graph generation

examples.desc: Live CPU usage by function (like top for CPU functions)
Count hardware events for a running process
Record 30 seconds of call stacks for a process
Display top CPU-consuming functions from recording

commands.pro_tip: Combine `perf record -g` with FlameGraph scripts (`perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > flame.svg`) to generate visual CPU flame graphs — the most powerful way to find hot code paths.

commands.name: bpftrace
commands.summary: Dynamic tracing of Linux kernel and userspace using eBPF.
commands.risk_reason: Incorrect programs can panic the kernel; requires root.
cautions: Needs root; a bad program or very frequent probes can degrade production performance.
Limit the runtime (interval:s:10 { exit(); }) and avoid tracing hot paths.
commands.explanation: bpftrace is a high-level tracing language for eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter). It instruments kernel events, tracepoints, uprobes, and kprobes without kernel modules or reboots. Enables tracing any function call in the kernel or any userspace process.

examples.desc: Trace every file opened, with process name

commands.pro_tip: Use bpftrace before strace in production — strace uses ptrace (process-attach, ~3x slower), while bpftrace uses eBPF (in-kernel, negligible overhead). Safe to run on live production.
